title: Chapter 20 — All Astir
paragraphs: A day or two passed, and there was great activity aboard the Pequod. Old sails were being mended, new sails were coming on board, along with bolts of canvas and coils of rigging. Everything indicated that the ship's preparations were hurrying to a close. Captain Peleg seldom or never went ashore, but sat in his wigwam keeping a sharp eye on the crew. Bildad handled all the purchasing and provisioning at the shops. And the men working in the hold and up in the rigging kept at it long after dark.

The day after Queequeg signed the articles, word was sent to all the inns where the crew was staying that their sea chests had to be on board before nightfall — there was no telling how soon the ship might sail. So Queequeg and I brought our belongings down, though we planned to sleep ashore until the last possible night. But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases, and the ship didn't actually sail for several more days. No surprise there — there was a great deal to be done, and no telling how many details needed attending to before the Pequod was fully equipped.

Everyone knows what a multitude of things — beds, saucepans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nutcrackers, and whatnot — are indispensable for running a household. It's just the same with whaling, which requires three years of housekeeping on the open ocean, far from all grocers, costermongers (street sellers of fruit and vegetables), doctors, bakers, and bankers. This is true of merchant ships too, but nowhere near to the same extent as with whalers. Besides the great length of the voyage and the many specialized items needed for the whale hunt, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors these ships usually visit, you have to remember that of all ships, whalers are the most exposed to accidents of every kind — especially the destruction and loss of the very equipment on which the voyage's success depends. Hence the spare boats, spare spars, spare lines and harpoons, and spare almost everything — everything but a spare captain and a duplicate ship.

By the time we arrived at the island, most of the Pequod's heavy stores had already been loaded — her beef, bread, water, fuel, iron hoops, and barrel staves. But as I mentioned, there was a constant stream of odds and ends, both large and small, being carried on board.

Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once the ship was fairly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for the small of someone's rheumatic back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a sister of charity, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

But it was startling to see this kind-hearted Quaker woman come aboard on the last day carrying a long oil ladle in one hand and an even longer whaling lance in the other. Nor were Bildad and Captain Peleg any less busy. Bildad carried a long checklist of needed supplies, and at every delivery, he made a mark next to that item on his list. Every now and then, Peleg hobbled out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up at the riggers on the masthead, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the ship, and each time I asked about Captain Ahab — how he was and when he planned to come aboard. They always answered that he was getting better and better and was expected any day. In the meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could handle everything needed to ready the vessel. If I had been truly honest with myself, I would have seen plainly that I only half liked the idea of being committed to such a long voyage without once laying eyes on the man who would be its absolute dictator the moment the ship reached open sea. But when a man suspects something is wrong, it sometimes happens that, if he is already caught up in the matter, he unconsciously tries to cover up his suspicions even from himself. And that's exactly what I did. I said nothing and tried to think nothing.
At last the word came that the ship would definitely sail the next day. So the following morning, Queequeg and I got a very early start.
